title: How to Get the Most from AI This Summer
dek: It's a summer weekend, so NLW goes action-oriented: a walkthrough of Ethan Mollick's refreshed "which AI to use to do stuff" guide, plus the launch of AIDB's choose-your-own-adventure Summer Adventure training. The through-line is one big behavioral shift — working with AI now looks a lot more like managing a team than chatting with a bot.

oneIdea.headline: The skill now is managing agents, not chatting with a bot.
oneIdea.summary: Ethan Mollick's updated guide draws a bright line between two interaction patterns: the old back-and-forth chat, where almost any model will do, and the new agentic workflow, where you delegate hours of work to a system that plans and acts on its own. That second pattern isn't just a new tool — it requires reprogramming how you think about AI. AIDB's free Summer Adventure is built to help you close your own "capability overhang": the gap between what AI can already do and what you're actually using it for.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Draft, never send — the permissions lesson is the clinical one
items.body: The sharpest detail in this edition is that Mollick's two agents behaved differently on the same instruction: Claude drafted a reply, ChatGPT actually sent an email, because it had been granted send permission earlier and never asked again. Transpose that into a surgery and it stops being an anecdote. A scribe that drafts and waits is a wholly different clinical risk from an agent that files a referral, orders a test or messages a patient. The workable rule for general practice is the one Mollick arrives at the hard way: leave everything set to ask for approval until you know the system's failure modes, and make every output land in a queue with a named clinician accountable for it. If NLW is right that delegation is the real skill, the delegation still has to end at a human signature.

items.title: The 195 references, and what would actually count as evidence
items.body: Thirty minutes of work, 195 references chased down, no invented page numbers — impressive, and precisely the sort of result that tells a practice manager nothing yet. The NHS question is not whether an agent can produce good work in a demonstration but what its error rate looks like under audit, on your patients, on a Monday morning. If Zitron is right that these stories are cargo cult in miniature, the discipline is cheap to adopt anyway: before buying anything agentic, decide in advance the number you would measure — letters returned for correction, coding errors, minutes per consultation — and measure it before and after. That one habit protects you whichever man turns out to be right.

items.title: Close your own overhang, but be slow with the practice cheque book
items.body: There is a real asymmetry worth naming. For an individual GP the capability overhang is genuine and almost free to close: better prompting of the scribe you already have, dictating letters differently, using the tool on the correspondence that eats your evenings. For a practice or a PCN the same enthusiasm becomes a procurement decision with a contract attached, and that is where Zitron's warning bites hardest. Note too what Mollick did to make the agents useful — he connected them to Gmail and a Google Drive. Nothing patient-identifiable belongs in a general consumer connector, and any such link needs a DPIA and the usual information-governance route first, not afterwards.

the_other_side.text: Zitron's answer to "you have a capability overhang" is that the overhang is a story told by people who need you to keep buying. In his account the tech industry has become a cargo cult, "people doing impressions of things that have worked before", and AI adoption is the purest example: executives who do not do the work mandate the tools because someone they admire said to. He is blunt about the demand side too, arguing the popularity of AI "has come entirely from social pressure and endlessly-discounted access", and that the moment real prices arrived customers started asking about ROI. He reads the industry's sudden enthusiasm for agentic loops as a revenue mechanism rather than a discovery, noting that Anthropic's Claude Code lead is allowed to burn upwards of a hundred and thirty thousand dollars a month in tokens, and saying flatly that it is unclear what benefits a loop might have.

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men circle is the gap between what AI can be shown doing and what it can be shown paying for. Both accept the demos are real: Zitron never disputes that a model checked Mollick's 195 references, he disputes that such anecdotes aggregate into economics. The empirical question that will resolve is whether skilled agentic use survives unsubsidised pricing, and the observable is renewal and seat-expansion on full-price agent tiers once free credits stop. The residue is pure worldview: whether slow uptake is a learning curve or a polite name for not worth the money. NLW is vindicated if heavy users keep paying real prices and firms show margin gains; Zitron is vindicated if usage falls away when the discounts do. Both are polemicists with skin in the game: NLW is launching a training programme premised on your overhang, Zitron sells subscriptions premised on certain collapse. Where they agree is the signal, and both say executives mandating AI they do not understand is a genuine failure mode. Watch full-price retention.

headlines.headline: Using AI now means two very different things
headlines.summary: Mollick's new guide splits AI use into two categories: the old chatbot back-and-forth, and agentic systems that can do the equivalent of many hours of human work in one go by pairing a model's brains with tools that let it plan and act. As he puts it, an agentic system basically gives an AI a computer to use.

headlines.headline: For low-stakes answers, any model will do
headlines.summary: For quick, low-stakes tasks like asking for a recipe or help drafting a letter, Mollick says nearly any model — including the free ones — is good enough. For anything you really care about, use a premier model set to a high thinking level.

headlines.headline: Only two real choices for serious work: ChatGPT or Claude
headlines.summary: When it comes to intensive agentic work, Mollick argues there are effectively only two options right now — ChatGPT or Claude. Notably, that means Gemini is officially out of his rankings, at least for now.

headlines.headline: Google… has fallen behind where it now counts.
headlines.attribution: Ethan Mollick, "An opinionated guide to which AI to use to do stuff"
headlines.summary: Mollick writes that Google, which led on benchmarks not long ago, has no leading frontier model and nothing close to Codex or Claude Code — which is why he doesn't suggest Gemini as a primary system, though he notes that could change quickly.

headlines.headline: The real unlock is connecting AI to your stuff
headlines.summary: Mollick's nudge is to actually use connectors — he's wired his systems into email, a non-private Google Drive, and many other apps. The "harness" he's describing is the set of controls and permissions that shape what the models can do, without ever using the word.

headlines.headline: "Prep for my seminar" — and the agents just went to work
headlines.summary: Mollick told both ChatGPT and Claude to connect to Gmail and prep his MBA seminar, including building demos and answering messages. Both correctly figured out the target Monday was in September, did web research, built teaching materials, and drafted responses — returning results in about 10 minutes that would've taken hours.

headlines.headline: Permissions matter a lot — one agent sent the email
headlines.summary: In the seminar test, Claude only drafted a reply while ChatGPT actually sent an email to a colleague — because Mollick had previously granted it send permission. His lesson: until you trust a system and understand its mistakes, leave everything set to ask for approval first.

headlines.headline: Computer use lets AI literally take over your machine
headlines.summary: With computer-use turned on in Claude Code or Codex, the AI can control your mouse, browser, and computer. Mollick had it download Blender — a program he doesn't know how to use — and model an otter using a laptop on an airplane. He flags it as a security concern to approach carefully.

headlines.headline: 195 references checked, zero hallucinations
headlines.summary: Mollick fed the full PDF of his professionally edited upcoming book to the AI, which worked 30 minutes, chased down 195 references, and returned pages of accurate notes — no invented page numbers, no fake text. His only complaint: it was too nitpicky, which he overrode with human judgment.

headlines.headline: Working with these systems is more like managing than it is chatting.
headlines.summary: Mollick's framing: you can almost think of AI agents as a team you delegate work to. NLW's read is that this is the core reprogramming required — a big shift in working, not just a new set of skills.

headlines.headline: Google isn't useless — just not your main driver
headlines.summary: Even while dropping Gemini from his primary recommendations, Mollick points to Google's Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM) and richer media models like a video-capable Gemini model as things worth using.

headlines.headline: Mollick is making agent-management feel approachable
headlines.summary: NLW's take: rather than going model-by-model, Mollick draws a bright line between the old chat pattern and the new managing-agents pattern — deliberately making agent management feel accessible to people whose eyes glaze over at words like "harness." It's simple on purpose, because he's writing for a far less mature AI audience.

headlines.headline: AIDB launches a free "Summer Adventure" training
headlines.summary: The new self-directed program at summeradventure.ai is a choose-your-own-adventure to expand your AI skills, following earlier AIDB programs like New Year, Claw Camp, and Agent OS. It's organized around 20+ travel-themed "destinations," each a lab or project teaching a new skill.

headlines.headline: Beginner to advanced, filterable by topic
headlines.summary: Destinations span beginner, intermediate, and advanced, filterable by level or by topic — tools, agents and automation, building and creating, or setting up knowledge and context. Complete a project and you "stamp your passport," which can stay private or be shared publicly.

headlines.headline: From day tripper to globetrotter
headlines.summary: The gamified tiers: one stamp makes you a "day tripper," three a "certified AI explorer," six a "trailblazer," and 10 a "globetrotter." NLW's own verdict on the naming: "Is that the height of millennial cringe? Yes. Do I care? Not even a little."

headlines.headline: "Pack Your ID" — build a portable profile of yourself
headlines.summary: A beginner "quick trip" project has you build a paste-ready global identity block of 150-300 words so any AI starts a chat already knowing who you are. Each lab ships with instructions, copyable prompts, an extension (e.g. teaching the AI how to push back on you), and a stretch goal.

headlines.headline: Building your first app is the biggest unlock
headlines.summary: NLW argues that vibe-coding your first application is one of the biggest unlocks available right now — more than almost anything else, it shifts you from seeing AI as an assistant that speeds up current work to something that unlocks entirely new capabilities. "Excursions" are projects that build something outlasting a single session.

headlines.headline: "Lemonade Stand": build an AI-staffed micro business
headlines.summary: This flagship "expedition" runs three sprints: mining 5-8 ideas from your history and skills down to a ranked top three; mapping one into a real micro business with an AI org chart and week-one task list; and validating demand with a thin demo before overbuilding. NLW says even happy employees gain from designing a full micro business.

headlines.headline: "The Loop": agentic loops for non-technical work
headlines.summary: The Loop expedition helps you build an actual agentic loop in a useful area of work — harder and less intuitive than in software engineering. It front-loads background learning on what a loop is and isn't, costs, models, how loops fail, and how to run one in tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex.

headlines.headline: Everyone has a capability overhang
headlines.summary: NLW's closing thesis: the 2026-defining idea is the capability overhang — the gap between what AI can do and what we're actually using it for. Almost no one is exempt, not even lab researchers or full-time AI content creators, because capabilities keep racing ahead faster than anyone can adopt them. The Summer Adventure is meant to help you close your own gap and have fun doing it.
